opening.say: Every time one of your cells divides, it needs a full copy of its DNA, and the copy has to be almost perfect.
DNA is a double strand, like a twisted ladder, and each rung is a pair of letters that always match up.
Because the letters pair up in a fixed way, each strand secretly holds the complete recipe for the other strand.

more.say: Say one strand reads A, A, G, C. Its partner has to read T, T, C, G, and nothing else will fit.
So if you split the ladder down the middle, you haven't lost anything. Each half still tells you exactly what its missing partner looked like.
That's the trick the cell uses. It doesn't memorize the whole sequence. It just uses each old strand as a pattern for a new one.

plan.setup: Watch what happens when the ladder unzips.
plan.narration: [[unzip]]An enzyme called helicase unzips the ladder. [[template]]Each old strand now acts as a template. [[pairing]]Free letters line up against it, A with T, G with C. [[polymerase]]An enzyme called DNA polymerase links them into a new strand. [[two-copies]]The result is two identical double helices, each with one old strand and one new.
plan.plan:
unzip: the double helix ladder splits down the middle from one end, two strands pulling apart into a Y shape.
template: the two separated strands are highlighted, each labeled as a template, with bare letters showing.
pairing: loose letters drift in and snap onto each template, A beside T, G beside C, matching colors.
polymerase: a blob labeled DNA polymerase slides along a strand, joining the new letters into a continuous chain.
two-copies: two complete double helices sit side by side, each showing one old strand in blue and one new strand in orange.
plan.close: Why does it matter that each new helix keeps one old strand?
